t: St. Brendan's Hospital has 41 night nurses on payroll.
Every night at midnight, the badge scanner at the main entrance records 42. I was the auditor sent to find the extra one.
By 3 in the morning I had found her.
And she knew my name.
But I should start at the beginning.
My name is Marcus Hale and I audit hospitals: billing errors, staffing records, missing medication.
It is quiet work, mostly spreadsheets and bad coffee.
St. Brendan's had flagged something strange.
Payroll said 41 night nurses.
The security system said 42 badges entered every night at exactly midnight.
Nobody could explain it. Nobody wanted to.
The hospital administrator met me at the front desk at 11 p.m. She was a tired woman with her coat already on as if she planned to leave the moment I arrived.
She handed me a visitor badge and a ring of keys.
Walk the floors, she said.
Count the staff. Check every badge against the roster.
I asked her where she was going. Home, she said.
I don't work nights here anymore.
Then she paused at the door and added one more thing without turning around.
Whatever happens at midnight, Mr. Hale, don't ask her name.
I laughed. She didn't.
The night staff gathered at the nurses station on the third floor.
41 people in blue scrubs holding paper cups.
I stood in front of them with my clipboard and felt like a substitute teacher on the first day.
The head nurse, a broad man named Dennis with a gray beard introduced me quickly.
Nobody smiled. Nobody asked questions.
A few of them were looking at the clock above the desk.
It was 11:48 p.m. I started with the roster. 41 names.
I read them aloud and each nurse raised a hand.
It took 10 minutes. Everything matched.
Every face had a name. Every name had a badge.
Then I noticed the note taped to the wall beside the telephone.
Yellow paper. Black marker.
A handwriting so shaky it looked like it had been written in the dark.
Never ask her name after midnight. Never ask what she is charting.
Count us every hour. I turn to Dennis.
What is this? He took off his glasses and wiped them slowly.
House rules, he said.
Whose rules?
The ones that keep us employed.
The clock above the desk clicked.
11:59 p.m. The nurses stopped talking.
One of them, a young woman named Priya, quietly set down her coffee.
Dennis moved to the door and stood very straight like a soldier waiting for inspection.
12 o'clock.
At the far end of the corridor, the elevator opened with a soft chime.
Nobody stepped out.
The doors stayed open for five seconds.
Then they closed.
And behind me, on the monitor of the badge scanner, a new line appeared.
Staff count 42. I turned around slowly.
The nurses were standing exactly as before.
41 of them, motionless.
Eyes fixed on the floor.
I counted them aloud to be sure.
There, Dennis whispered.
You see? I see 41. And the scanner sees 42. I looked at the monitor again.
The entry had a stamp.
Timestamp: 12:00:00.
No badge number.
No photograph.
Only a small gray silhouette, the kind the system shows when a picture is missing.
Who is she? I asked.
Priya made a tiny sound, almost a whimper.
Dennis put a finger to his lips.
You can't ask that, he said, not out loud.
Behind him, at the end of the hallway, a light turned on in a room that had been dark a minute earlier.
Room 312. I took my flashlight and walked toward it.
Nobody followed me.
The corridor smelled like disinfectant and something sweeter, like old flowers.
The floor tiles squeaked under my shoes.
Halfway there, I heard a voice.
A woman humming softly.
A lullaby, slow and out of tune.
I stopped outside the door.
It was open about a hand's width.
I pushed it with two fingers.
A nurse stood at the foot of a bed holding a clipboard, her back to me.
She wore a white uniform, old-fashioned, with a small cap pinned to her hair.
The kind I had only seen in photographs.
The bed was empty, but she was writing on the chart anyway, nodding as if somebody were answering her questions.
Excuse me, I said.
The humming stopped.
She didn't turn around.
She tilted her head slightly, as if listening to something far away.
Then she said very gently, you're early tonight, Marcus.
I had not given her my name.
I stepped back so fast I hit the doorframe.
The nurse didn't move.
She just kept writing.
The pen scratching against paper.
The sound too loud in the silence.
I remembered the rule.
Never ask her name.
So I asked something else.
What are you charting?
The pen stopped.
The room grew cold instantly.
The way a room does when someone opens a freezer.
She slowly lowered the clipboard to her side.
Oh, she whispered.
You shouldn't have asked that.
Then the light in the room went out.
I ran.
I ran down the corridor until I reached the nurse's station, where Dennis was already waiting with a stone-faced stare.
You asked her, he said.
I asked what she was charting.
He closed his eyes. That's almost as bad.
Priya was crying silently now.
The other nurses had gathered around the desk.
Arms crossed, shoulders tense.
Someone had turned the clock face down.
Listen to me, Dennis said.
She walks the rounds every night.
She never hurts the patients.
She never touches us. She only charts.
Charts what?
The ones who are about to die.
I looked at him.
Go check, he said quietly.
Room 312. The chart she wrote. I didn't want to.
But I'm an auditor. I trust documents.
So I went back, shaking, and found the clipboard lying on the empty bed.
The paper was yellowed.
Brittle at the edges.
The handwriting was neat and slanted.
A list of names, each with a date and a time.
At the top, Mrs. Eleanor Wynne.
Below it, Mr. Alvarez.
And at the very bottom, the last line, written in fresh ink that's still shown wet under the flashlight.
Marcus Hale.
Stairwell B.
12 o'clock a.m.
I read it three times. It was already past one.
I ran to the patient in room 308. Mrs. Wynne was asleep.
Her breathing shallow, but steady.
I stood beside her for an hour, watching the monitor.
At 312, her heart stopped.
Dennis and Priya rushed in.
They worked on her for 20 minutes, but she was already gone.
When it was over, Dennis looked at me with something that was almost pity.
She's never wrong, he said.
That's why we count every hour.
If the number you're seeing is 42, it means she's chosen someone.
Chosen how? She doesn't kill them, Priya said softly.
She just writes their name, and then the hospital takes care of the rest.
I thought of the last line on the chart.
Marcus Hale. Stairwell B.
It said midnight, I said.
But it's three in the morning.
I'm still alive.
Dennis frowned. That's strange.
Why? Because she's never been late.
I decided to check the staff roster again to compare it with the badge records.
I went back to the administrator's office, opened the filing cabinet and found the personnel folders.
Every nurse had one.
41 folders in alphabetical order.
At the end of the drawer, there was a 42nd folder, thin and gray without a label.
I opened it. Inside was a single sheet of paper, an employee file, a photograph stapled to the corner.
It was my face.
The name read Marcus Hale, R.N. Night Shift.
Third floor, date of hire is 11 years ago.
Date of termination, 3 years ago.
And under that, in a different handwriting deceased on duty, cardiac arrest.
Stairwell B, 12 o'clock a.m.
My hands went numb.
The paper slipped between my fingers and landed on the floor.
I didn't remember being a nurse.
I remembered an apartment, a car, an office with fluorescent lights.
I remembered audits and invoices and coffee.
But I couldn't remember my mother's face or my last birthday.
Or any day before the administrator handed me the visitor badge at 11 p.m.
I turned around.
The old-fashioned nurse stood in the doorway.
The white cap tilted.
Her face finally lifted into the light.
She looked exactly like Priya, 30 years older.
You always come back, she said kindly.
Every night you arrive as someone new.
An auditor. A visitor.
A repairman. And every night you try to count us.
Why? My voice cracked.
Why do I come back? Because you never finished your rounds.
I looked at my badge. The visitor's tag was gone.
In its place hung a plastic card with a small photograph and the name Marcus Hale, R.N.
The extra nurse on the scanner wasn't her.
It was me.
The ghost who walked the corridors at midnight, 42 on the count, was the nurse who had died in stairwell B three years ago and never left.
Then who are you?
I whispered. She smiled, and for the first time I saw the exhaustion in her eyes. The same exhaustion I had seen on the administrator's face.
I'm the one who stayed to help you remember, she said.
Every night I write your name.
Every night you survive another round.
And every night you forget again.
And if I stop forgetting?
Then someone has to take your place.
The clock in the hall struck four. Priya and Dennis stood behind her now, quiet, waiting.
41 nurses in blue scrubs lined along the corridor, watching me with eyes full of tired kindness.
We never told you, Dennis said.
Because the last time we did you ran into the stairwell and didn't come back for a year.
I looked down the hall. At the end, a door marked Stairwell B stood slightly open,
a faint white light spilling out of it. What happens if I go in?
You finally rest, Priya said.
But then the count drops to 41 and the scanner stops recording the extra badge.
The hospital stops needing night nurses.
And the patients?
They'd have no one to chart them, the old nurse said gently.
No one to warn them. No one to sit beside them when the monitors fail.
I understood then.
The extra nurse was not a curse.
She was a watchman, a ghost who kept the rounds so nobody else had to die alone. And I was the one who couldn't let go.
At 5 a.m. the front doors opened and the day shift arrived. The administrator walked in carrying her coffee.
Young and rested, wearing her coat over a clean uniform.
Mr. Hale, she said brightly.
Did you find the extra nurse?
I looked at the clipboard in my hand.
The audit form was blank. The visitor badge was gone, and my reflection in the glass door showed a man in blue scrubs,
pale, exhausted, with a name tag that read R.N.
Yes, I said quietly.
I found her. She smiled, relieved. Good. Then we can close the case. She turned and left the building. Behind me the elevator chimed.
At 11 that night, a new auditor stepped through the front door, carrying a leather bag.
Young, nervous, wearing a visitor badge too large for his coat.
I walked to the nurse's station and picked up a black marker.
I tore a sheet of yellow paper from the pad and in shaky handwriting, wrote the rule.
Never ask her name after midnight.
Never ask what she is charting. Count us every hour.
I taped it to the wall beside the telephone and waited. At 11.59 the new auditor looked at the clock above the desk.
Is something supposed to happen?
I smiled and for the first time I felt no fear. Don't ask her name, I said gently. She'll tell you when she's ready.
